One small step for this week, then a simple 90-day path, built around your top career match
Your chosen direction: Artificial Intelligence
Your choice

Your strengths in learning, communication, and leadership fit well with AI roles that involve working with teams, explaining technical ideas clearly, and picking up new tools quickly — skills that matter a lot in this field. That said, your top RIASEC types are artistic, social, and conventional, which means you may enjoy creative and people-facing work more than deep solo coding, so a role like AI product analyst or AI project lead may suit you better than a pure machine-learning engineering role.
GAP TO CLOSE

Most AI roles in Bahrain expect you to know programming in Python and to understand basic machine learning concepts — that is, how computers learn patterns from data — which may go beyond what a general information systems degree covers. You will likely need to fill this gap with focused self-study or a short course before you are competitive for technical AI positions.

Based on general market trends in Bahrain, AI-related roles are growing but still relatively limited in number, and most employers at entry level expect candidates to show a portfolio of small projects or certifications alongside their degree — this is a general outlook, not verified job-market data.
Your first step this week

Find 5 real entry-level or junior AI-related job postings on Bahraini job boards such as Bayt or LinkedIn filtered to Bahrain, and write down the exact skills, tools, and qualifications each one asks for. Why: Seeing real postings tells you what employers in Bahrain actually want right now, which is more useful than guessing. It also helps you compare those requirements against what your information systems degree already gave you, so you know exactly what to focus on.
YOU WILL PRODUCE
A simple two-column list: on one side, what the job asks for; on the other side, which of those things you already have from your degree or work experience. This becomes your personal gap list.
WHEN
Day 1 — set aside about 60 minutes, it is free, and you can do it alone on any device.
Worksheet:
Looking at the 5 postings, which 3 skills or tools appear most often that you do not yet have from your studies?
Which parts of your information systems coursework or past work experience match something at least one employer is asking for?
Based on the job titles you found, which type of AI role seems closest to what you want to do day-to-day — more technical, more analytical, or more project-focused?
Days 2–7

Days 2-3 — It would help to take your two-column gap list and write a one-page summary of your degree, your 1-3 years of experience, and any projects you completed that touch on data, systems, or technology. This becomes the raw material for your CV. You will produce: A rough one-page professional summary document that you can use as the base for a full CV.

Day 4 — A good use of this day is to draft a proper CV using your summary, making sure the skills and tools you already have are clearly listed and matched to the language you saw in the job postings. Free CV templates are available on most job platforms. You will produce: A first draft of your CV, tailored toward AI or data-related roles, ready for feedback.

Days 5-6 — We suggest asking one person — a former classmate, a lecturer, or a colleague from your work experience — to read your CV draft and give you honest feedback, then make at least 3 specific improvements based on what they say. You will produce: A revised CV with at least 3 clear improvements noted, and a short list of the feedback you received.

Day 7 — A good way to end the week is to review what you produced and pick the next step. You will produce: A short written note — even a few bullet points — summarising what your CV now shows, which gaps still need filling, and one concrete thing you will do in week 2 to move forward.
Your next 90 days
Weeks 2–4 — Build momentum

Taking a free beginner course in Python for data analysis — available on several free online learning platforms — would help you start filling the most common technical gap employers ask for, and completing even the first few lessons gives you something concrete to mention on your CV.

It would be worthwhile to set up or update a profile on a professional networking platform, list your information systems background and your interest in AI, and connect with at least 5 people in Bahrain who work in technology or data roles — this is not about asking for a job, just about making your presence visible in the local tech community.

Working through one small, self-directed project — for example, downloading a public dataset and writing a short report on patterns you find — would give you a basic portfolio item to show employers, which matters more than many candidates realise at the entry level.
Months 2–3 — Build

Preparing for and sitting a recognised entry-level certification such as the Microsoft Azure AI Fundamentals (AI-900) or the IBM AI Foundations for Everyone certificate would show employers a formal, verifiable signal that you understand core AI concepts, and both are achievable without years of prior AI experience.

It would help to start attending any technology or AI-related meetups, workshops, or events held in Bahrain — government and private sector organisations in the country do run these from time to time — because meeting people working in the field gives you a much clearer picture of what local employers actually look for day-to-day.

A good use of months 2 and 3 is to apply to at least 3 entry-level or junior roles in Bahrain that match your updated CV — even roles with titles like data analyst, systems analyst, or technology associate that sit next to AI work — so you get real feedback from the application process and can adjust your materials accordingly.
Your skills to build and practice exercise: Artificial Intelligence
SKILLS TO BUILD

Evaluating and improving AI outputs — AI tools can produce code, designs, reports and written content quickly, but they often make mistakes or miss context — being able to check, correct and improve what AI produces is what makes your work reliable and trusted.

Prompt writing — giving clear instructions to AI systems — Almost every career on your list now involves asking AI tools to help with something; the quality of what you get back depends almost entirely on how clearly and specifically you ask, so this is a practical skill that transfers across all of these roles.
PRACTICE EXERCISE

A good exercise would be to pick a real task from any of your career interests — for example, writing a short user research summary, a basic security risk list, or a simple app feature description. First, write your own version without any AI help, even if it takes only ten minutes. Then, open a free AI chat tool and give it a prompt asking it to do the same task. Compare the two versions side by side: note where the AI was more complete, where it was wrong or too general, and what you had to fix or add. Then write a short paragraph explaining the three most important decisions you made when editing the AI version.
YOU WILL HAVE

You will have a before-and-after document — your original version, the AI version, and your edited final version — plus a short note explaining your decisions. This is something you can show to a future employer to demonstrate that you can use AI tools critically, not just blindly.
